why.correct: The renal pelvis is the funnel at the center of the kidney, formed where the major calyces join. It narrows into the ureter as it leaves the hilum.
options: Correct. The funnel that collects urine from the major calyces is the renal pelvis.
A major calyx is one of the two or three large cups that empty into this funnel, not the funnel itself.
The renal sinus is the space inside the hilum, filled with fat, that holds the pelvis and vessels. It is not the urine-filled funnel.
The ureter is the tube that continues from the funnel outside the kidney, down toward the bladder.

why.correct: Renal columns are bands of cortex-like tissue that reach inward between the pyramids. The interlobar arteries and veins run through them.
options: A renal pyramid is the striped cone of medulla on either side of this band, not the band between them.
A renal papilla is the rounded tip of a pyramid, pointing into a minor calyx.
Correct. The tissue between two pyramids is a renal column.
A minor calyx is the cup around a papilla, part of the urine-collecting system.

why.correct: A minor calyx is the small cup that surrounds the tip of one renal papilla and receives the urine dripping from it.
options: A major calyx is larger and forms where several minor calyces join.
Correct. The small cup around a papilla is a minor calyx.
The renal papilla is the tip of the pyramid that this cup surrounds.
The renal pelvis is the central funnel that the major calyces empty into.

why.correct: Arcuate arteries arch along the boundary between cortex and medulla, over the base of each pyramid. They come from the interlobar arteries and give off the cortical radiate arteries.
options: Interlobar arteries run outward between the pyramids, through the renal columns, before they bend into arches.
Segmental arteries are the first branches of the renal artery, in the renal sinus near the hilum.
Cortical radiate arteries run straight out from the arches into the cortex, toward the surface.
Correct. The artery arching over the base of a pyramid is an arcuate artery.

why.correct: Segmental arteries are the first branches of the renal artery, in the renal sinus. Each supplies one segment of the kidney and does not connect with its neighbors.
options: Correct. The renal artery divides into about five segmental arteries.
The renal artery is the single vessel from the aorta that enters at the hilum, before it divides.
Interlobar arteries are the next branches, running out between the pyramids.
Arcuate arteries are further out, arching over the bases of the pyramids.

why.correct: The pudendal nerve is a somatic nerve from S2 to S4. Its motor neurons release acetylcholine onto the skeletal muscle of the external urethral sphincter and keep it closed until you decide to empty your bladder.
options: The vagus nerve carries parasympathetic fibers to organs of the chest and upper abdomen, not to the bladder or its sphincters.
The pelvic splanchnic nerves carry parasympathetic fibers that contract the detrusor. They supply smooth muscle, not the skeletal muscle of the external sphincter.
Correct. The pudendal nerve drives the voluntary external urethral sphincter.
The femoral nerve supplies the front of the thigh, not the pelvic floor.

why.correct: The renal artery enters at the hilum and divides into segmental arteries in the renal sinus. These give interlobar arteries, which run between the pyramids, then arcuate arteries, which arch over the pyramid bases, then cortical radiate arteries, which run out into the cortex.

Urine drips from the renal papilla into a minor calyx. Minor calyces join into a major calyx, and the major calyces empty into the renal pelvis, which narrows into the ureter. The ureter carries urine to the bladder, and the urethra carries it out.

Stretch starts the signals. They reach the pons and cortex, and when the cortex allows it, the pontine center switches the bladder from storing to emptying. Pudendal firing falls first, so the external sphincter relaxes. A few seconds later, the sacral micturition center's parasympathetic fibers fire, the detrusor contracts and the internal sphincter opens, so urine flows.
Interlobar arteries (inter- = between) run outward between the pyramids, through the renal columns, from the segmental arteries to the arcuate arteries.
options: Correct. Interlobar arteries link the segmental and arcuate arteries.
The inferior vena cava receives blood from the renal veins; it is not on the arterial path into the kidney.
The abdominal aorta is where the renal artery comes from, before this path begins.
The gonadal artery is a separate branch of the aorta to the testis or ovary; it is not part of the path inside the kidney.

why.correct: The renal fascia is the outer sheet that anchors the kidney. Inside it is the adipose capsule, the cushion of fat. The renal capsule is the thin, tough layer stuck to the kidney's surface.
options: This is the right list read backward: the renal capsule is the innermost layer, on the kidney's surface.
The adipose capsule lies inside the renal fascia, not outside it.
The fat lies between the fascia and the capsule; the renal capsule is stuck directly to the kidney.
Correct. Fascia, then fat, then the capsule on the surface.

why.correct: Segmental arteries are end arteries: each supplies its own segment, and neighboring segmental arteries do not join. When one is blocked, no other vessel can bring blood in, so the wedge of tissue it fed dies.
options: Clots in arteries travel toward smaller arteries, not backward from the veins. The problem is the lack of any alternative arterial route.
Correct. With no connections between segmental arteries, a blocked one leaves its segment without blood.
The cortex is full of capillaries and receives most of the kidney's blood flow; they are downstream of the blocked artery.
The fat cushions the kidney from outside. It does not squeeze arteries shut.

why.correct: The kidneys are retroperitoneal: they lie against the muscles of the back wall of the abdomen, with the peritoneum covering only their front surfaces. A surgeon coming from behind reaches the kidney before reaching the peritoneum.
options: Organs on a mesentery, such as most of the small intestine, lie inside the peritoneal cavity. The kidneys are not among them.
The kidneys sit high, from about T12 to L3, above the iliac crest.
Correct. Being retroperitoneal lets a surgeon reach the kidney from behind.
Only the upper part of each kidney is covered behind by the 11th and 12th ribs; the rest lies below them.

why.correct: Each ureter runs obliquely through about 2 cm of bladder wall. When the bladder fills or contracts, its pressure flattens that slanted tunnel, which works as a one-way valve: a peristaltic wave can push urine in, but bladder pressure cannot force it back out.
options: The ureters have smooth muscle, not a skeletal-muscle sphincter. The valve comes from their slanted path through the wall.
Correct. The oblique passage through the bladder wall acts as a valve.
The trigone is a smooth triangle of lining on the bladder floor. It does not seal the ureter openings by contracting.
Peristalsis moves urine down the ureters in any position, including lying down.

why.correct: Bacteria near the urethral opening have only 3 to 4 cm to travel to reach a woman's bladder, compared with about 20 cm in a man, and the male urethra also has two bends.
options: Both sexes have a trigone, the smooth triangle between the ureter openings and the urethral opening.
Both sexes have an external urethral sphincter of skeletal muscle in the pelvic floor.
Correct. A much shorter urethra gives bacteria a much shorter route to the bladder.
In both sexes, the ureters enter the back of the bladder.

why.correct: The drug removes the parasympathetic drive on the detrusor. Contractions weaken, so the bladder holds more before urgency and may empty less completely. The voluntary external sphincter works through a different receptor protein and is unaffected.

variables.name: Strength of detrusor contractions
variables.why: Parasympathetic fibers contract the detrusor by releasing acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptor proteins. Blocking those receptor proteins weakens the contraction.

variables.name: Volume the bladder holds before an urgent need to empty
variables.why: With weaker, less frequent detrusor contractions, the bladder can fill further before pressure rises enough to force an urgent need to empty.

variables.name: Strength of the external urethral sphincter
variables.why: The external sphincter is skeletal muscle driven by the pudendal nerve through nicotinic receptor proteins, which this drug does not block.

variables.name: Volume left in the bladder after emptying
variables.why: A weaker detrusor contraction may not empty the bladder fully, so more urine can be left behind.

why.correct: The liver fills the upper right part of the abdomen, so the right kidney sits about 1 to 2 cm lower than the left.
options: Correct. The large liver above it pushes the right kidney down a little.
The heart lies in the thorax, above the diaphragm, and tilts to the left. It does not reach the kidneys.
The aorta lies slightly to the left of the midline; the inferior vena cava is on the right.
The two kidneys are about the same size. Their difference in height comes from the liver.

why.correct: Renal columns are bands of tissue between the pyramids that carry blood vessels. Urine never passes through them. The step after the minor calyx should be the major calyx.
options: Correct step. Urine leaves the kidney tissue through tiny openings on the renal papilla.
Correct step. The minor calyx cups the papilla and receives the urine.
This is the wrong step. Renal columns are tissue between the pyramids, not part of the collecting system; the major calyx belongs here.
Correct step. The major calyces empty into the renal pelvis.
Correct step. The renal pelvis narrows into the ureter.
Correct step. The ureter carries urine to the bladder.

why.correct: The bladder is a stretchy muscular bag behind the pubic bone. Its wall is the detrusor muscle, its lining is transitional epithelium that folds into rugae when empty, and the smooth triangle of the trigone joins the ureter openings to the urethral opening.
options: Correct. The detrusor is the smooth muscle of the bladder wall.
Correct. Transitional epithelium lines it and folds into rugae when the bladder is empty.
Correct. These three openings are the corners of the trigone.
Correct. The bladder sits in the pelvic cavity just behind the pubic bone.
The trigone is the one part of the lining that stays smooth. It has no rugae.

why.correct: The muscle you squeeze on purpose to hold in urine is the external urethral sphincter, skeletal muscle in the pelvic floor, driven by the pudendal nerve. Voluntary tightening is lost when that nerve is damaged, while the parasympathetic supply that contracts the detrusor still works.
options: Her bladder still contracts normally, so the parasympathetic supply to the detrusor is working.
The internal sphincter is smooth muscle under involuntary control. She never tightened it on purpose.
The trigone is lining, not a muscle she could squeeze.
Correct. Losing voluntary squeezing points to the pudendal nerve and the external sphincter.

why.correct: The kidneys make urine out of plasma. Their blood flow is set far above their own oxygen needs, and it is the large volume of plasma passing through them each minute that lets them adjust the blood's water, salt and wastes.
options: Kidney cells do use a lot of oxygen, but the blood flow is several times what they need. The flow is mainly raw material for urine.
The kidneys do not heat the blood; core temperature is set by metabolism in organs throughout the body.
The veins, not the kidneys, hold most of the body's blood reserve.
Correct. The kidneys process plasma, so they need a large flow of it.

why.correct: The glomerular capsule (Bowman's capsule) is the hollow cup around the glomerulus, the swollen start of the tubule. Filtered fluid collects in the space inside it.
options: The glomerulus is the tuft of capillaries inside the cup, not the cup itself.
Correct. The cup wrapped around the capillary tuft is the glomerular capsule.
The proximal convoluted tubule is the coiled tube that leaves the capsule at the tubular pole.
The afferent arteriole is the blood vessel that carries blood into the capillary tuft.

why.correct: The efferent arteriole carries blood out of the glomerulus and on into the peritubular capillaries. It is an arteriole, not a venule.
options: The afferent arteriole carries blood into the glomerulus from the cortical radiate artery.
A venule drains the peritubular capillaries later. The vessel leaving the glomerulus is still an arteriole.
Correct. The vessel leaving the glomerulus and feeding the peritubular capillaries is the efferent arteriole.
The cortical radiate artery is the larger vessel that the afferent arteriole branches from.

why.correct: The nephron loop (loop of Henle) is the hairpin part of the tubule that dips toward the medulla and climbs back, with a descending and an ascending limb.
options: Correct. The hairpin segment of the tubule is the nephron loop.
The collecting duct is the wide, straight duct that many nephrons drain into, not a hairpin.
The distal convoluted tubule is the coiled segment back in the cortex, after the loop.
The vasa recta are blood vessels that run beside long loops. The pin marks the tubule itself.

why.correct: Peritubular capillaries (peri- = around) are the mesh of low-pressure capillaries wrapped around the tubules in the cortex. They are fed by the efferent arteriole and take up what the tubule returns.
options: The glomerulus is the first capillary bed, a compact tuft inside the capsule, not a mesh around the tubule.
Arcuate veins run along the boundary between cortex and medulla, far larger than these capillaries.
The vasa recta are long, straight hairpin capillaries in the medulla. This mesh wraps the coiled tubules.
Correct. The capillary mesh around the tubules is the peritubular capillaries.

why.correct: The macula densa (dense spot) is a patch of tall, crowded cells in the wall of the tubule where it touches its own arterioles. They sense how much sodium chloride is in the fluid flowing past.
options: Juxtaglomerular cells sit in the wall of the afferent arteriole, not the tubule, and release renin.
Podocytes wrap the glomerular capillaries inside the capsule.
Correct. These tubule cells are the macula densa.
Mesangial cells lie between the arterioles and inside the glomerulus, not in the tubule wall.

why.correct: Juxtaglomerular (granular) cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole. Their granules store renin, which they release into the blood.
options: Correct. The renin-releasing cells in the arteriole wall are the juxtaglomerular cells.
The macula densa is in the tubule wall. It signals to these cells but does not release renin itself.
Hepatocytes are liver cells. They release angiotensinogen, the protein renin acts on.
Chromaffin cells are in the adrenal medulla and release epinephrine.

why.correct: Fluid filtered from the glomerulus collects in the capsular space of the glomerular capsule, flows into the proximal convoluted tubule, down the descending limb and up the ascending limb of the nephron loop, through the distal convoluted tubule, and into a collecting duct.

The afferent arteriole branches off the cortical radiate artery and feeds the glomerulus. The efferent arteriole carries blood out to the peritubular capillaries, which drain through venules into the cortical radiate vein.
Blood leaves the glomerulus through the efferent arteriole, which then feeds the second capillary bed, the peritubular capillaries.
options: A venule would drain a capillary bed toward the veins. Here blood still has a second capillary bed to cross, so the vessel between them is an arteriole.
Correct. The efferent arteriole links the two capillary beds.
The vasa recta are a second capillary bed like the peritubular capillaries, fed by the efferent arteriole; they do not come between the glomerulus and the peritubular capillaries.
Cortical radiate veins are much larger vessels that collect blood after both capillary beds.

why.correct: The vasa recta are blood vessels running beside long loops, not part of the tubule. After the proximal convoluted tubule, fluid enters the descending limb of the nephron loop.
options: Correct step. Filtered fluid first collects in the capsular space.
Correct step. It then flows into the proximal convoluted tubule.
This is the wrong step. The vasa recta carry blood; the descending limb of the nephron loop belongs here.
Correct step. Fluid climbs back toward the cortex in the ascending limb.
Correct step. The distal convoluted tubule follows the loop, back in the cortex.
Correct step. The distal tubule drains into a collecting duct.

why.correct: This is the proximal convoluted tubule. Microvilli multiply the surface area for transport, and mitochondria supply the ATP that its pumps use. It takes back most of the filtered water and solutes.
options: Urine is stored in the bladder, lined by transitional epithelium. No tubule segment stores urine.
Many mitochondria mean heavy ATP use. A segment built only to let water through would not need them.
Renin comes from juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole wall, not from tubule cells.
Correct. A large surface and plenty of ATP point to heavy transport, which is the proximal tubule's job.

why.correct: The renal corpuscle is the glomerulus plus the glomerular capsule. The capsule has a parietal layer, a visceral layer of podocytes and the capsular space between them.
options: Correct. The glomerulus is the capillary tuft of the corpuscle.
Correct. Podocytes form the capsule's visceral layer on the capillaries.
Correct. The capsular space collects the filtered fluid.
The macula densa is in the wall of the tubule where it returns to the corpuscle. It is part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus, not the corpuscle.
The proximal convoluted tubule starts where the corpuscle ends, at the tubular pole.
Correct. The parietal layer is the outer wall of the capsule.

why.correct: Juxtamedullary nephrons have their corpuscles in the inner cortex, next to the medulla, and long loops that plunge deep into the medulla, served by the vasa recta.
options: Every nephron has a proximal convoluted tubule.
All renal corpuscles are in the cortex. Juxtamedullary ones sit in the inner cortex, next to the medulla.
Both kinds drain into collecting ducts, which carry urine to the papilla.
Correct. The long loop is what defines a juxtamedullary nephron.

why.correct: Long loops, like those of juxtamedullary nephrons, are what let a kidney make urine more concentrated than blood. Desert animals that must save water have very long loops.
options: The pyramids hold the loops and collecting ducts that concentrate urine. Losing them would make concentrating harder, not easier.
Short loops contribute little to concentrating urine. An animal that saves water this well needs long ones.
Every glomerulus drains through an efferent arteriole; without one, blood could not leave the glomerulus.
Correct. Very long loops go with very concentrated urine.

why.correct: Most capillary beds drain into venules, which offer little resistance. The glomerulus drains into the efferent arteriole, a resistance vessel, so pressure backs up in the glomerular capillaries.
options: The kidneys are no closer to the heart than many other organs. The layout of their vessels, not distance, sets the pressure.
Glomerular capillaries are thin, leaky fenestrated capillaries. Wall thickness does not raise the pressure inside.
Correct. Resistance downstream, in the efferent arteriole, keeps glomerular pressure high.
Podocytes wrap the capillaries; they do not pump. The heart supplies the pressure.

why.correct: Juxtaglomerular cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole wall. They are stretch-sensitive: when less pressure stretches the arteriole, they release more renin. Sympathetic stimulation after the bleed adds to this.
options: The macula densa senses sodium chloride in the tubule fluid, not arteriole pressure, and it signals the renin-releasing cells rather than releasing renin itself.
Podocytes form part of the filter around the capillaries. They do not release renin.
Proximal tubule cells take back filtered fluid. They do not release renin.
Correct. The juxtaglomerular cells sense the lower stretch and release renin.

why.correct: Each collecting duct receives fluid from the distal tubules of many nephrons and carries it through the medulla to the papilla.
options: Each distal convoluted tubule belongs to one nephron.
Correct. Collecting ducts are shared by many nephrons.
Each proximal convoluted tubule belongs to one nephron and leads from its own capsule.
Each glomerular capsule surrounds one glomerulus and belongs to one nephron.

why.correct: Podocytes (pod- = foot) form the visceral layer of the glomerular capsule. Their branches wrap each glomerular capillary and interlock, leaving narrow gaps that are part of the filter.
options: Correct. Podocytes wrap the capillaries as the capsule's visceral layer.
That describes a juxtaglomerular cell.
That describes a macula densa cell.
The outer wall is the parietal layer, a simple squamous epithelium. Podocytes line the inner, visceral layer.

why.correct: The two capillary beds of a nephron are in series: afferent arteriole, glomerulus, efferent arteriole, peritubular capillaries. Blocking the first vessel starves everything downstream in that nephron but leaves its neighbors untouched.

variables.name: Blood flow into its glomerulus
variables.why: The afferent arteriole is the only way blood enters the glomerulus, so blocking it stops the flow.

variables.name: Fluid entering its capsular space
variables.why: With no blood and no pressure in the glomerulus, nothing is pushed into the capsule.

variables.name: Blood flow in the peritubular capillaries fed by its efferent arteriole
variables.why: The efferent arteriole receives its blood from the glomerulus, so the second capillary bed downstream loses its supply too.

variables.name: Blood flow into the glomerulus of a neighboring nephron
variables.why: Each nephron has its own afferent arteriole from the cortical radiate artery, so a clot in one does not block the others.

why.correct: Mesangial cells sit between the glomerular capillary loops. They hold the loops in place, can contract to change the filtering surface, and engulf debris trapped by the filter. A few more lie outside the glomerulus in the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
options: Correct. Support, contraction and clean-up are their jobs.
Renin comes from juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole wall.
Sensing sodium chloride is the job of the macula densa in the tubule wall.
The capsular space is lined by the parietal layer and the podocytes of the capsule.

why.correct: Nephrons are not replaced after birth. The remaining ones enlarge and each handles more fluid, so total kidney work falls less than the number of nephrons, until too few are left.
options: You are born with all the nephrons you will have; lost ones are not replaced.
Correct. Surviving nephrons take on extra work, which hides the loss for a time.
Collecting ducts have no glomeruli, so they cannot filter blood.
The bladder's transitional epithelium seals urine in; it does not take back water and salt.

why.correct: NFP = GBHP − (CHP + BCOP) = 60 − (15 + 32) = 60 − 47 = +13 mm Hg. Positive, so fluid is filtered into the capsule.
options: Correct. 60 − 47 = +13 mm Hg.
107 comes from adding all three pressures. Capsular pressure and colloid osmotic pressure oppose filtration, so they are subtracted.
45 comes from subtracting only the capsular pressure (60 − 15). The colloid osmotic pressure of 32 mm Hg also pulls fluid back.
The sign is reversed. The outward pressure, 60, is larger than the inward total, 47, so NFP is positive.

why.correct: NFP = 55 − (25 + 30) = 55 − 55 = 0 mm Hg. With no net outward pressure, filtration stops. A blockage anywhere downstream raises capsular pressure and opposes filtration.
options: Capsular pressure opposes filtration, so extra pressure in the capsule lowers filtration rather than raising it.
Correct. 55 − 55 = 0, so filtration stops.
Capsular hydrostatic pressure is one of the three pressures in the equation. Raising it lowers NFP.
Capsular pressure pushes fluid back into the capillaries, not out of them.

why.correct: GFR = Kf × NFP = 12 mL/min/mm Hg × 8 mm Hg = 96 mL/min. The mm Hg units cancel.
options: 20 comes from adding the two numbers. GFR is their product.
1.5 comes from dividing 12 by 8. Multiply them instead.
Correct. 12 × 8 = 96 mL/min.
960 is ten times too large: 12 × 8 is 96.

why.correct: Constricting the afferent arteriole cuts off pressure and flow before the glomerulus. Glomerular pressure, NFP and GFR all fall, along with renal blood flow and the pressure in the capillaries downstream.

variables.name: Renal blood flow
variables.why: Narrowing a vessel in series with the whole kidney raises resistance, so less blood flows through.

variables.name: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure
variables.why: More pressure is lost across the narrowed afferent arteriole before blood reaches the glomerulus.

variables.name: Net filtration pressure
variables.why: NFP = GBHP − (CHP + BCOP). GBHP falls while the opposing pressures stay the same.

variables.name: GFR
variables.why: GFR = Kf × NFP, and NFP has fallen.

variables.name: Hydrostatic pressure in the peritubular capillaries
variables.why: Less pressure passes through the glomerulus and efferent arteriole to the capillaries downstream.

why.correct: Narrowing the exit from the glomerulus raises pressure inside it, so GFR rises even though total flow falls. A larger fraction of the plasma is filtered, which concentrates the proteins in the blood reaching the peritubular capillaries. If the constriction were severe, the protein concentration would climb so high along the glomerulus that GFR would fall instead.

variables.name: Renal blood flow
variables.why: The efferent arteriole is in series with the rest of the kidney's vessels, so narrowing it raises total resistance and lowers flow.

variables.name: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure
variables.why: Blood backs up behind the narrowed exit, so pressure in the glomerular capillaries rises.

variables.name: GFR
variables.why: Higher GBHP raises net filtration pressure, and with moderate constriction that outweighs the slower flow.

variables.name: Filtration fraction
variables.why: GFR rises while renal plasma flow falls, so a larger share of the plasma is filtered.

variables.name: Colloid osmotic pressure in the peritubular capillaries
variables.why: More protein-free fluid has been filtered out of the same plasma, so the proteins left in it are more concentrated.

why.correct: Between about 80 and 180 mm Hg the solid curve is almost flat. Autoregulation narrows the afferent arterioles as pressure rises, so GFR rises only slightly, from about 123 to about 129 mL/min.
options: A 60 percent rise would be the dashed line's behavior. The solid curve, with autoregulation, is nearly flat here.
Correct. On the plateau, GFR hardly changes.
The curve does not fall at 160 mm Hg. The arterioles narrow just enough to offset the pressure, not enough to close.
The dashed line shows what would happen without autoregulation. The question asks about the solid curve.

why.correct: Below about 80 mm Hg the afferent arterioles have widened as far as they can, so autoregulation can no longer make up for the low pressure. The partial widening still keeps GFR above the dashed line, but GFR now falls with pressure. Strong sympathetic activation after a bleed lowers it further.
options: A more permeable membrane would raise GFR, not lower it. Nothing in a bleed makes the filter leakier.
Autoregulation is still helping at point A: the curve sits above the dashed line. It has reached its limit, not switched off.
Correct. Autoregulation is at its limit, so GFR falls with pressure, though less than it would without it.
Nothing in a bleed raises capsular pressure. The problem is the low pressure reaching the glomerulus.

why.correct: Filtration slits are the narrow gaps between the interlocking pedicels of neighboring podocytes. A thin slit diaphragm bridges each one.
options: Fenestrations are pores through the endothelial cells of the capillary, on the blood side of the basement membrane.
Correct. The gaps between pedicels are filtration slits.
Intercellular clefts are gaps between endothelial cells in ordinary capillaries, not between podocyte branches.
The capsular space is the whole cavity of the capsule that the filtrate enters, not the gaps in the podocyte layer.

why.correct: Fenestrations (fenestra = window) are round pores through the endothelial cells of the glomerular capillaries. They are large enough to let all dissolved substances through but stop blood cells.
options: Filtration slits are gaps between podocyte pedicels, on the capsule side of the basement membrane.
Tight junctions join neighboring endothelial cells at their edges; they are not pores through the cells.
Pedicels are the podocytes' finger-like branches, not holes in the capillary.
Correct. The pores through the endothelium are fenestrations.

why.correct: After a large bleed, the baroreceptor reflex drives strong sympathetic activity. Norepinephrine on alpha-1 receptor proteins constricts the afferent arterioles, glomerular pressure falls, and GFR and urine output drop, which saves blood volume.
options: Correct. Strong sympathetic activation overrides autoregulation and lowers GFR.
After blood loss the atria are less stretched, not more, so ANP release falls.
Lower plasma protein would weaken the inward pull and raise GFR, not lower it.
Tubuloglomerular feedback dilating the afferent arterioles would help GFR, not cause it to fall.

why.correct: When fluid is low, sympathetic activity and angiotensin II are high and tend to clamp the afferent arterioles. Locally made prostaglandins keep them open. Ibuprofen blocks prostaglandin synthesis, so the afferent arterioles narrow, glomerular pressure falls and GFR drops. In a healthy person prostaglandins do little to GFR, so the drug has little effect.
options: Even at high doses, the sharp fall in GFR here comes from the arterioles, not from damage to the podocytes or the filtration slits.
Nothing about ibuprofen blocks the flow of urine, so capsular pressure is unchanged.
Efferent constriction would raise glomerular pressure, not lower GFR, and it is not how ibuprofen acts.
Correct. Removing the protective prostaglandins lets the afferent arterioles narrow.

why.correct: With narrowed renal arteries, little pressure reaches his glomeruli. Angiotensin II was constricting his efferent arterioles and backing pressure up into the glomeruli, which kept him filtering. Blocking its production relaxes the efferent arterioles, glomerular hydrostatic pressure falls, and GFR drops.
options: Correct. Losing the efferent constriction lowers glomerular pressure and GFR.
Angiotensin II is a vasoconstrictor. Having less of it relaxes arterioles; it does not constrict them.
ACE inhibitors act on the arterioles through angiotensin II, not on the filter's permeability.
ACE inhibitors lower aldosterone, and in any case aldosterone acts on the tubules, not on GFR.

why.correct: Small solutes such as glucose, urea, sodium and amino acids cross all three layers of the filter freely, so their concentrations in the filtrate match plasma. Cells and large proteins such as albumin are held back.
options: Correct. Glucose is small and filtered freely; the tubules take it back later.
Albumin is mostly held back by the basement membrane and the slit diaphragms; only a trace gets through.
Correct. Urea is a small molecule and is filtered freely.
Blood cells are stopped by the fenestrated endothelium.
Correct. Sodium and other small ions pass freely.
Correct. Amino acids are small and are filtered freely.

why.correct: Faster flow leaves less time to take back sodium chloride, so more reaches the macula densa. Its cells release ATP, which becomes adenosine and constricts the afferent arteriole. Less pressure reaches the glomerulus, and GFR falls back toward normal: negative feedback.

The glomerular basement membrane, formed from the fused basement membranes of the endothelium and the podocytes, lies between the two cell layers. It is thick and negatively charged, and it holds back large proteins.
options: Correct. The basement membrane sits between the endothelium and the podocytes.
The parietal layer is the outer wall of the capsule, across the capsular space, not part of the filter.
The capsular space is where the filtrate ends up, after all three layers.
Mesangial cells lie between the capillary loops; filtrate does not pass through them.

why.correct: Calcium entry makes the smooth muscle contract, so the afferent arteriole constricts, not dilates. Constriction loses more pressure before the glomerulus, which keeps glomerular pressure near normal.
options: Correct step. A rise in pressure starts the response.
Correct step. Higher pressure stretches the arteriole wall.
Correct step. Stretch opens mechanically gated channels, and calcium enters.
This is the wrong step. Calcium makes the muscle contract, so the arteriole constricts.
Correct step. The constriction offsets the higher pressure.

why.correct: Diabetes damages the glomerular basement membrane and podocytes, so albumin leaks into the urine (proteinuria). As plasma albumin falls, blood colloid osmotic pressure falls. In capillaries throughout the body, less protein holds fluid in the blood, filtration outpaces drainage, and edema appears.
options: Protein in urine does not act on the bladder to cause fluid retention. The link is through plasma albumin.
His problem is a leaky filter, not less filtration. The swelling comes from low plasma protein.
Correct. Low albumin weakens the inward pull in every capillary, causing edema.
A little extra protein in the filtrate does not force fluid into the veins; the loss of protein from the blood is what matters.

why.correct: Red cells squeezed through an inflamed filtration membrane come out misshapen, and the tubules mold them into cylinder-shaped plugs. Protein leaking through the same damaged filter usually comes with them. This pattern points to the glomeruli.
options: Bleeding from the urethra gives normal-shaped red cells, not plugs molded by tubules, and usually no heavy protein loss.
Blood from the bladder enters after the tubules, so it cannot be molded into tubule-shaped plugs.
Correct. Misshapen cells, tubule-molded plugs and proteinuria all point to a damaged filter.
The renal pelvis lies after the tubules; blood entering there is not shaped by them and does not bring heavy protein loss.

why.correct: Filtration fraction = GFR ÷ renal plasma flow = 120 ÷ 600 = 0.20, or 20 percent. One fifth of the plasma reaching the glomeruli is filtered; the rest leaves in the efferent arterioles.
options: 5 comes from dividing the wrong way round (600 ÷ 120). The fraction filtered is GFR divided by plasma flow.
50 percent would mean half the plasma is filtered. 120 is one fifth of 600, not half.
480 mL/min is the plasma that is not filtered (600 − 120), not the fraction that is.

why.correct: About a fifth of the plasma is filtered as it passes through the glomerulus, and the filter holds back the proteins. The same amount of protein ends up in less plasma, so its concentration, and the oncotic pull it produces, rise along the capillary.
options: The liver releases albumin into the general circulation, not into the glomerulus specifically. The rise happens within one pass through the glomerulus.
Correct. Removing protein-free fluid concentrates the proteins that remain.
Podocytes wrap the capillaries from outside and are part of the filter. They do not add protein to the blood.
Blood cells do not break down as they pass through a healthy glomerulus.

why.correct: ANP widens the afferent arteriole, raising glomerular hydrostatic pressure, and relaxes mesangial cells, increasing the filtering surface. GFR rises, and more sodium and water leave in the urine, lowering blood volume.
options: Constricting the afferent arteriole is what strong sympathetic activity does. ANP does the opposite.
Correct. Both effects raise GFR.
Mesangial contraction is an effect of angiotensin II. ANP relaxes mesangial cells.
ANP is released by the heart but acts on the kidneys, the adrenal cortex and blood vessels.

why.correct: At the moment pressure falls, glomerular pressure and GFR dip. Within seconds, the myogenic mechanism and tubuloglomerular feedback widen the afferent arterioles, and both return almost to normal. The same signals raise renin release, which starts the body-wide response to the lower pressure.

variables.name: Diameter of the afferent arterioles
variables.why: Less stretch relaxes their smooth muscle (myogenic mechanism), and less sodium chloride at the macula densa lowers adenosine release (tubuloglomerular feedback), so the afferent arterioles widen.

variables.name: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure
variables.why: It dipped at first, but the wider afferent arterioles lose less pressure, bringing it back almost to normal.

variables.name: GFR
variables.why: 85 mm Hg is still on the plateau, so autoregulation returns GFR almost to its old value.

variables.name: Renin release
variables.why: Less stretch of the afferent arteriole and less sodium chloride at the macula densa both make the juxtaglomerular cells release more renin.

why.correct: A normal GFR is about 125 mL/min. Over 1,440 minutes that is about 180 L a day, of which more than 99 percent is taken back.
options: 1.5 L a day is a typical urine output, what is left after the tubules take back most of the filtrate.
125 is the GFR per minute, not per day.
18 L is ten times too small.
Correct. 125 mL/min × 1,440 min ≈ 180 L a day.

why.correct: The fenestrations in the endothelium, about 70 to 100 nm across, are far smaller than any blood cell, so cells stay in the capillary. The deeper layers hold back proteins.
options: Blood cells never reach the filtration slits; they are already stopped at the first layer.
The parietal layer is the outer wall of the capsule, not part of the filter.
Cells are stopped before reaching the basement membrane, which mainly holds back proteins.
Correct. The endothelium's pores are too small for cells.

why.correct: Water reabsorbed = 170 − 1.7 = 168.3 L. As a share of the water filtered: 168.3 ÷ 170 = 0.99, or 99%.
options: 1% is the share that leaves as urine (1.7 ÷ 170), not the share reabsorbed.
90% would leave 17 L of urine a day, ten times what she passes.
Correct. 168.3 of 170 L comes back to the blood.
10% is the share that would be reabsorbed if most of the filtrate became urine; she passes only 1.7 L.

why.correct: Filtered load = GFR × plasma concentration = 180 × 140 = 25,200 mmol/day. Reabsorbed = filtered − excreted = 25,200 − 200 = 25,000 mmol/day, about 99.2%.
options: 25,200 mmol is the filtered load. Some of it, 200 mmol, is excreted, so less than that is reabsorbed.
25,400 comes from adding the excreted sodium to the filtered load. Excreted sodium is subtracted.
320 comes from adding 180 and 140. The filtered load is their product, not their sum.

why.correct: Glucose enters by secondary active transport: it rides in with sodium, which flows down the gradient that the basolateral pump makes. With the pump stopped, sodium leaks in and is not removed, the gradient runs down, and the symporters have nothing to drive them.
options: Correct. The pump spends the ATP; the symporters spend the sodium gradient it makes.
The carriers need no ATP directly, but they need the sodium gradient, and only the pump maintains it.
Sodium building up inside the cell lowers the gradient into the cell, which slows the symporters rather than speeding them.
The paracellular route is passive and carries no glucose against its gradient. Glucose in the lumen falls to near zero, below plasma, so it could not diffuse back that way.

why.correct: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs about 65% of filtered sodium and water, plus nearly all glucose and amino acids.
options: The loop reabsorbs about 25% of sodium and 15% of water: a lot, but less than the proximal tubule.
Correct. About two thirds of both come back here.
The distal tubule reabsorbs only about 5% of the sodium and very little water.
The collecting duct handles the last few percent. It decides the final urine but moves the least volume.

why.correct: At 600 mg/dL the filtered line reads 750 mg/min and the reabsorbed line is flat at the transport maximum, 375 mg/min. Excreted = 750 − 375 = 375 mg/min, which is where the excreted line sits.
options: 750 mg/min is the filtered load. Half of it is still reabsorbed.
Correct. Filtered minus the transport maximum: 750 − 375.
Excretion is zero only below the renal threshold, about 180 mg/dL.
About 190 mg/min is what the excreted line shows near 450 mg/dL, not 600.

why.correct: Glucose is always filtered. At 280 mg/dL, he is above the renal threshold of about 180 mg/dL: nephrons with fewer carriers for their load are saturated, and glucose passes them into the urine.
options: Glucose is small and is filtered freely by healthy glomeruli at any blood level. Filtration of glucose is normal; what fails is reabsorbing all of it.
Glucose is not secreted by the tubule. It is filtered, then reabsorbed on sodium–glucose symporters.
Correct. His filtered load is above the renal threshold, so reabsorption can't keep up everywhere.
The tubule reabsorbs glucose with sodium symporters that work without insulin. Insulin controls glucose uptake into muscle and fat.

why.correct: The 300 mg/dL figure assumes every nephron saturates at the same moment. They don't: nephrons with fewer carriers for their filtered load spill glucose early. That produces the curved splay on the graph between about 180 and 350 mg/dL.
options: Correct. Uneven nephrons make the kidney as a whole leak before its average limit.
The calculation already uses the GFR, and a small rise in GFR would not move the threshold down by 120 mg/dL.
Glucose is not secreted by the tubule; at normal levels urine glucose is zero.
The transport maximum is set by the number of carriers, which does not fall as glucose rises; the flat part of the graph stays at 375 mg/min.

why.correct: Aldosterone acts on principal cells: more sodium channels, potassium channels and pumps. Sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion both rise, so the body keeps sodium and loses potassium. The proximal tubule's glucose handling is not affected.

variables.name: Number of open sodium channels in principal cells
variables.why: Aldosterone makes principal cells build more apical sodium channels, potassium channels and basolateral pumps.

variables.name: Sodium reabsorbed in the collecting duct
variables.why: More channels and pumps move more sodium from the lumen into the blood.

variables.name: Potassium secreted into the urine
variables.why: Sodium entering the principal cells leaves the lumen more negative, and the extra potassium channels let more potassium leave the cells into the urine.

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: Potassium lost in urine exceeds intake, so plasma potassium falls, sometimes to hypokalemia.

variables.name: Glucose reabsorbed in the proximal tubule
variables.why: Aldosterone acts on principal cells at the end of the tubule. Glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule is unchanged.

why.correct: The pump makes the sodium gradient; the symporter spends it to bring glucose in; glucose concentrates in the cell; it leaves down its own gradient on a basolateral carrier; and it enters the peritubular capillary, whose low hydrostatic and high colloid osmotic pressure favor uptake.

Potassium (by principal cells), H+ (by the proximal tubule and intercalated cells) and drugs such as penicillin (by organic acid carriers in the proximal tubule) are secreted. Glucose and amino acids are filtered and reabsorbed; albumin is mostly held back by the filter.
options: Correct. Principal cells secrete it, and nearly all the potassium in urine comes from that secretion.
Glucose is filtered and reabsorbed, never secreted.
Correct. Proximal tubule carriers for organic acids secrete penicillin.
Amino acids are filtered and then reabsorbed on sodium symporters.
Correct. The proximal tubule and intercalated cells secrete it.
Albumin is a large protein that the filtration membrane mostly holds back. It is not secreted.

why.correct: The thick ascending limb is nearly impermeable to water, so water cannot follow the salt. That is exactly why the fluid leaving it is dilute.
options: This step is right. That is the stoichiometry of the Na–K–2Cl cotransporter.
This step is right. Potassium recycling keeps NKCC2 supplied and charges the lumen positive.
This step is right. The positive lumen drives paracellular reabsorption of calcium, magnesium and sodium.
This is the error. Water stays in the lumen, because this segment has almost no aquaporins.
This step is right. Salt out, water in: the fluid falls to about 100 mOsm/L.

why.correct: Tubular secretion adds a substance to the tubular fluid, so it is added to what was filtered and not reabsorbed.
options: Correct. Secretion adds to the amount excreted.
Diffusion is a way substances move, including during reabsorption; it is not a separate term in the balance.
The tubule cells do metabolize a few substances, but the standard balance for excretion is filtered − reabsorbed + secreted.
The tubule does not store substances; it passes them to the blood or the urine.

why.correct: Principal cells carry the sodium channels, potassium channels and pumps that aldosterone increases. Blocking aldosterone lowers their sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion, so the drug makes the body lose sodium and keep potassium.
options: Intercalated cells handle acid–base balance and respond mainly to blood pH.
Podocytes form the filtration slits of the glomerular capsule; they don't reabsorb sodium.
Proximal tubule cells respond to angiotensin II and PTH; aldosterone's main target is further along.
Correct. Principal cells are aldosterone's target.

why.correct: Excreted = filtered − reabsorbed + secreted. More is excreted than was filtered, so there must be net secretion: 120 − 50 = 70 mg/min at least, more if some is also reabsorbed.
options: Reabsorption would make the urine amount smaller than the filtered amount, not larger.
Without either process, excretion would equal filtration: 50 mg/min.
Filtration happens only in the glomerulus. The collecting duct cannot filter.
Correct. Only secretion can make excretion exceed filtration.

why.correct: NKCC2 pumps salt out of the thick ascending limb, and the segment is nearly waterproof, so solute leaves and water stays. The fluid gets more dilute as it rises.
options: The descending limb loses water to the salty medulla; that makes fluid more concentrated on the way down, not dilute.
Correct. Solute leaves, water stays, and osmolarity falls to about 100.
Water is not secreted; nothing in the tubule actively pumps water.
Almost no water crosses the wall of the thick ascending limb in either direction, and capillaries do not add water to tubular fluid.

why.correct: The paracellular route (para- = beside) runs between neighboring cells through their tight junctions. It is passive and needs no carrier. The proximal tubule's leaky tight junctions let water and small ions take it.
options: The transcellular route goes through a cell, across two membranes.
Endocytosis takes material into a cell in a vesicle; it is part of a transcellular route.
Correct. Between the cells.
Facilitated diffusion is a way to cross a membrane on a carrier, so it belongs to the transcellular route.

why.correct: The interstitial space lies between the tubule cell's basolateral membrane and the peritubular capillary. Everything the tubule reabsorbs passes through its fluid before entering the blood.
options: Correct. It is the thin fluid space between the cell and the capillary.
The lumen is on the other side of the cell, against the brush border.
The bloodstream is inside the capillary, beyond the interstitial space.
The brush border is the microvilli on the lumen side of the cell.

why.correct: Facultative water reabsorption depends on ADH putting aquaporins into principal cells. With less ADH, the collecting duct lets less water out, and a large volume of dilute urine follows.
options: The proximal tubule reabsorbs water whatever ADH does, because it is always permeable to water. That is why it is called obligatory.
The descending limb is always permeable to water, so its reabsorption is obligatory too.
Correct. Only this part is set by ADH.
The thick ascending limb reabsorbs essentially no water at any ADH level.

why.correct: PTH makes the kidney keep calcium, at the distal tubule, and lose phosphate, at the proximal tubule. Both help raise blood calcium without raising the calcium–phosphate product. Later, if PTH stays high and blood calcium rises, more calcium is filtered, and urine calcium can end up higher than normal.

variables.name: Calcium reabsorbed in the distal convoluted tubule
variables.why: PTH increases calcium reabsorption through channels in the distal tubule.

variables.name: Calcium in the urine
variables.why: More filtered calcium is reabsorbed, so less is left to leave in the urine.

variables.name: Phosphate reabsorbed in the proximal tubule
variables.why: PTH removes sodium–phosphate symporters from proximal tubule membranes.

variables.name: Phosphate in the urine
variables.why: Less phosphate is reabsorbed, so more is excreted.

why.correct: The blood has passed two arterioles, so its hydrostatic pressure is low, and a fifth of its plasma was filtered off while the proteins stayed, so its colloid osmotic pressure is high. Both favor fluid moving into the capillary.
options: High hydrostatic pressure with low colloid osmotic pressure would push fluid out of the capillary, the way the glomerulus filters.
Low hydrostatic pressure helps, but low colloid osmotic pressure would weaken the pull of fluid into the capillary.
Correct. Low push out, strong pull in.
High hydrostatic pressure would oppose uptake. Peritubular blood has already lost pressure through the afferent and efferent arterioles.

why.correct: Water leaves the collecting duct only by osmosis, so urine can at most reach the osmolarity of the medulla around the duct. With the papilla at 600, her urine tops out near 600 mOsm/L, however much ADH she has.
options: 1,200 mOsm/L needs a medulla at 1,200. No pump moves water, so the urine can't outrun its surroundings.
Correct. Her maximum urine concentration equals her medulla's.
300 mOsm/L is what the fluid would reach with a medulla no saltier than plasma. Her medulla still reaches 600.
50 mOsm/L is the most dilute urine, made when ADH is absent. Her ADH is high.

why.correct: Volume = solute ÷ concentration = 900 mOsm ÷ 1,200 mOsm/L = 0.75 L. He can't pass less without waste solute building up in his blood.
options: 0.5 L is the minimum for a 600 mOsm load. His load is larger, so his minimum is larger.
1.33 L comes from dividing 1,200 by 900, the wrong way round.
1.5 L is 900 ÷ 600: it assumes his urine can reach only twice plasma's osmolarity, but his kidneys reach 1,200 mOsm/L.

why.correct: Blocking ADH's receptor protein removes the collecting duct's aquaporins. The medullary gradient is still there, but water can't use it. A large volume of dilute urine follows, and the plasma becomes more concentrated until thirst makes the person drink.

variables.name: Aquaporins in the apical membranes of principal cells
variables.why: Without the ADH signal, cAMP falls and the cells pull their apical aquaporins back into vesicles.

variables.name: Water reabsorbed from the collecting duct
variables.why: With few apical aquaporins, the duct is nearly waterproof, so little water leaves it for the salty medulla.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Water that is not reabsorbed stays in the duct and leaves as urine.

variables.name: Urine osmolarity
variables.why: Dilute fluid from the thick ascending limb passes through the collecting duct without losing water, and gets more dilute still as sodium is reabsorbed.

variables.name: Osmolarity of the plasma
variables.why: The body loses more water than solute, so the solute left in the plasma is more concentrated.

why.correct: Blocking NKCC2 cuts reabsorption of about a quarter of filtered sodium and stops the multiplier, so the kidney can't concentrate urine. Urine volume rises, blood volume falls, and potassium is lost because more sodium reaches the principal cells.

variables.name: NaCl reabsorbed by the thick ascending limb
variables.why: The drug blocks NKCC2, the main carrier that moves salt out of that segment.

variables.name: Osmolarity of the inner medulla
variables.why: Salt is no longer pumped into the medulla, so the countercurrent multiplier stops and the vasa recta slowly carry the gradient away.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Sodium left in the tubule holds water with it, and a weaker gradient draws less water out of the collecting duct.

variables.name: Potassium in the urine
variables.why: More sodium and faster flow reach the principal cells, which reabsorb more sodium and secrete more potassium.

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: The extra salt and water lost in urine come out of the extracellular fluid, including the plasma.

why.correct: Losing water raises plasma osmolarity and lowers blood volume. The hypothalamus raises ADH, which opens the collecting duct to water, and the RAAS raises aldosterone, which keeps sodium. He passes a small volume of concentrated urine, but only drinking replaces what he lost.

variables.name: Osmolarity of the plasma
variables.why: He loses more water than salt, so the solute left behind is more concentrated.

variables.name: ADH release
variables.why: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors sense the rise in osmolarity, and the fall in blood volume adds to the signal.

variables.name: Aquaporins in collecting duct principal cells
variables.why: ADH acts through cAMP to insert stored aquaporins into the apical membrane.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Water leaves the collecting duct into the salty medulla and returns to the blood.

variables.name: Urine osmolarity
variables.why: The fluid in the collecting duct comes close to the medulla's 1,200 mOsm/L.

variables.name: Aldosterone release
variables.why: The fall in blood volume lowers pressure in the kidney's small arteries, so renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone rise.

why.correct: Osmoreceptors trigger ADH release; ADH binds its receptor protein on principal cells; cAMP and protein kinase A move aquaporins into the apical membrane; and water leaves the duct by osmosis into the concentrated medulla.

In the hairpin vasa recta, blood gains solute on the way down and gives it back on the way up, so it leaves with little extra. Blood flowing down and away would keep picking up salt and urea and never give them back, and the gradient would wash out.
options: Blood enters at 300 mOsm/L, less salty than the medulla, so it would remove salt, not add it.
The loops build the gradient, but it only lasts if blood flow does not carry it away. That is the exchanger's job.
Nothing would pump salt into the cortex. The gradient would flatten, not reverse.
Correct. The hairpin shape is what stops blood flow from carrying the gradient away.

why.correct: The medullary osmotic gradient climbs from about 300 mOsm/L at the cortex to about 1,200 mOsm/L at the papilla in humans.
options: 300 mOsm/L is the value in the cortex, the same as plasma.
Correct. Salt and urea bring it to about 1,200.
About 100 mOsm/L is the fluid leaving the thick ascending limb, inside the tubule.
Some desert rodents with very long loops reach this; human kidneys do not.

why.correct: Salt pumped out of the thick ascending limb and urea from the inner medullary collecting duct supply the solute. Countercurrent flow in the loop multiplies it into a gradient, and the vasa recta's hairpin keeps blood flow from washing it out.
options: Correct. This is the energy-using step of the multiplier.
Correct. Urea supplies about half the inner medulla's osmolarity.
The proximal tubule is in the cortex, and its glucose reabsorption doesn't add solute to the medulla.
Correct. Countercurrent flow is what multiplies the pump's small effect.
The thick ascending limb has almost no aquaporins. If water could follow the salt out, no gradient would form.
Correct. Countercurrent exchange preserves the gradient.

why.correct: The descending limb has few salt carriers and pumps nothing. Its fluid becomes concentrated because it loses water by osmosis.
options: This step is right. It is the multiplier's single active step.
This step is right. That is how the descending fluid comes to match the interstitial fluid.
This is the error. The descending limb concentrates its fluid by losing water, not by gaining salt through pumps.
This step is right. Countercurrent flow brings ever more concentrated fluid to the bend.
This step is right. The small difference at each level is multiplied along the loop.

why.correct: The descending limb is permeable to water but not much to salt, so water leaves by osmosis and the solute left inside becomes more concentrated.
options: Correct. Losing water concentrates the fluid.
Losing salt would make the fluid more dilute, not more concentrated.
Urea tends to enter the thin descending limb from the medulla, not leave it.
Losing potassium would lower the fluid's osmolarity, and the descending limb does not handle much potassium.

why.correct: With no ADH, the dashed line keeps falling through the collecting duct, to about 50 mOsm/L at its end. The duct keeps reabsorbing sodium but lets almost no water out.
options: The tip of the loop is where the fluid is most concentrated, 1,200 mOsm/L.
The fluid at the end of the proximal tubule is 300 mOsm/L, the same as plasma.
The start of the distal tubule is about 100 mOsm/L. With no ADH, it gets more dilute still after that.
Correct. About 50 mOsm/L.

why.correct: Solute leaves on carriers, and water follows at once by osmosis through aquaporins and leaky tight junctions. Because they leave together, volume falls but concentration stays at 300 mOsm/L.
options: The proximal tubule reabsorbs about 65% of filtered sodium and nearly all glucose and amino acids.
Correct. Solute and water leave together.
The tubule never secretes water; water moves only by osmosis, and here it moves out with the solute.
ADH acts on the collecting duct, not the proximal tubule, which is always permeable to water.

why.correct: High ADH with no response to extra ADH points to the kidney: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. A faulty ADH receptor protein or aquaporin on principal cells leaves the collecting duct waterproof, so dilute urine flows out despite the hormone.
options: Too little ADH would show a low ADH level, and synthetic ADH would fix it. His level is high and the injection fails.
Correct. The principal cells don't respond, so the collecting duct stays closed to water.
Filtering more would not explain a high ADH level that fails to act; the tubule would still reabsorb most of the extra.
More salt pumping would build a steeper gradient, helping concentrate urine, not diluting it.

why.correct: Thiazides block the sodium–chloride symporter in the distal convoluted tubule, and they make the distal tubule reabsorb more calcium. They lower blood pressure steadily and reduce calcium in the urine.
options: Loop diuretics remove the positive lumen of the thick ascending limb, so more calcium is lost in urine, the opposite of what she needs.
Osmotic diuretics are used short term, for example for brain swelling, and do not lower urine calcium.
Correct. Thiazides keep calcium.
Blocking ADH makes more dilute urine but doesn't lower blood pressure much, and it doesn't target calcium.

why.correct: Blocking NKCC2 leaves more sodium in the tubule. More sodium enters the principal cells of the collecting duct, leaving the lumen more negative, and the faster flow carries secreted potassium away, so more is secreted. A lower blood volume also raises aldosterone, adding to the loss.
options: Loop diuretics act on the thick ascending limb, not the proximal tubule.
Aldosterone increases potassium secretion, and a loop diuretic raises aldosterone by lowering blood volume. Less aldosterone would keep potassium, not lose it.
The drug is a blocker, not a pump. It acts by stopping NKCC2.
Correct. The potassium loss happens downstream, in the collecting duct.

why.correct: Urea comes from the breakdown of amino acids. With little protein, the liver makes less urea, less reaches the inner medullary collecting duct, and the inner medulla loses much of the urea that makes up about half its osmolarity.
options: Correct. Less urea recycling means a shallower inner medulla gradient.
ADH is a small peptide made in tiny amounts; a low-protein diet does not stop its release.
Nothing in the scenario points to lost carriers; the salt part of the gradient is intact.
Filtering less water would not limit how concentrated the urine can become.

why.correct: These vesicles hold aquaporins inside the principal cell. When ADH raises cAMP, they fuse with the apical membrane and put the water channels in place.
options: Correct. The stored water channels wait here until ADH acts.
An aquaporin is one water channel, drawn as a dot in the membrane. The pin marks the vesicle that holds them.
The interstitial fluid is the thin band between the cells and the blood vessel.
The lumen is the space inside the duct, on the other side of the cells.

why.correct: Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic. It is filtered, can't be reabsorbed, and its osmotic effect keeps water in the tubule, mainly in the segments always permeable to water, so more water leaves as urine.
options: That describes a loop diuretic such as furosemide.
Correct. Unreabsorbed solute holds water in the tubule.
Mannitol acts inside the tubule; it does not work by changing ADH.
That describes a potassium-sparing diuretic.

why.correct: The multiplier is the nephron loop: the thick ascending limb spends ATP, through NKCC2 and the sodium–potassium pump, to build the gradient. The exchanger is the vasa recta: only diffusion and osmosis, keeping blood flow from washing the gradient out.
options: Correct. Loop builds, vessels preserve.
This swaps the two. Blood vessels have no NKCC2 pumps.
The exchanger is the vasa recta, not the collecting duct, and it uses no energy directly.
ADH decides whether the collecting duct uses the gradient; it does not build it. The loop's pumps do.

why.correct: C = (U × V) ÷ P = (90 × 1.5) ÷ 1.0 = 135 mL/min. U and P are both in mg/dL, so their units cancel and the answer is in mL/min.
options: 60 comes from dividing U by V (90 ÷ 1.5). U must be multiplied by V to get the amount excreted.
Correct. 90 × 1.5 = 135, divided by 1.0.
1.35 is 100 times too small; mg/dL cancels with mg/dL, so no conversion is needed.
91.5 comes from adding U and V. Clearance multiplies them.

why.correct: First turn the volume into a flow: 2,880 mL ÷ 1,440 min = 2.0 mL/min. Then C = (60 × 2.0) ÷ 1.5 = 80 mL/min, below normal.
options: Correct. V = 2 mL/min, and 120 ÷ 1.5 = 80.
115,200 uses the whole day's volume as if it were a per-minute flow. Divide by 1,440 minutes first.
45 uses 1.5 mL/min for V and 2.0 for P, swapping them. V is 2.0 and P is 1.5.
120 is U × V without dividing by the plasma concentration.

why.correct: A clearance of zero means none reaches the urine. A freely filtered substance with zero clearance must be completely reabsorbed, as glucose and amino acids are at normal plasma levels.
options: Balanced secretion and reabsorption would leave the filtered amount in the urine, so clearance would equal GFR, not zero.
Correct. All of the filtered load returns to the blood.
The question says it is freely filtered.
Urine has no enzymes that destroy filtered nutrients; the zero reflects reabsorption in the tubule.

why.correct: Filtration alone would give a clearance equal to GFR, 120 mL/min. A clearance of only 40 means two thirds of what was filtered came back to the blood: net reabsorption.
options: Net secretion would push clearance above GFR.
Filtration alone, like inulin, gives a clearance equal to GFR.
Correct. Clearance below GFR means net reabsorption.
The urine volume is already built into the clearance value; comparing clearance with GFR is enough.

why.correct: He makes creatinine at the same rate, and at steady state excretes it at that rate: excretion ≈ GFR × plasma creatinine. For the product to stay the same while plasma creatinine doubles, GFR must have halved.
options: A higher GFR would clear creatinine faster and lower its plasma level.
A one-unit rise looks small, but creatinine and GFR move in inverse proportion; doubling the level means halving the GFR.
With steady production, a lasting rise in plasma creatinine means excretion per unit of plasma fell.
Correct. Double the creatinine, half the GFR.

why.correct: Creatinine is filtered freely and not reabsorbed, but a little is also secreted. The extra secreted creatinine in the urine makes its clearance a bit higher than the plasma actually filtered.
options: Correct. Secretion adds to filtration.
Reabsorption would make clearance lower than GFR, not higher.
Creatinine comes from creatine phosphate in muscle, not from the tubule.
Creatinine is small and filtered freely; proteins are held back by the filter.

why.correct: Hemorrhage lowers pressure. The baroreceptor reflex raises sympathetic drive, which constricts the afferent arterioles and releases renin; ADH rises steeply. GFR falls, and the tubule keeps sodium and water, so the man passes a small volume of concentrated, low-sodium urine while his kidneys conserve volume.

variables.name: Sympathetic activity to the kidneys
variables.why: Lower arterial pressure reduces baroreceptor firing, and the cardiovascular center raises sympathetic output.

variables.name: GFR
variables.why: Low arterial pressure falls below the range autoregulation can cover, and sympathetic nerves constrict the afferent arterioles.

variables.name: Renin release
variables.why: Less stretch of the juxtaglomerular cells and more sympathetic stimulation both raise renin.

variables.name: ADH release
variables.why: A volume loss of this size, about a quarter of blood volume, is far above the 5 to 10% that triggers ADH.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Less is filtered, and ADH and aldosterone make the tubule reabsorb more of what is filtered.

variables.name: Sodium in the urine
variables.why: Angiotensin II and aldosterone raise sodium reabsorption, and pressure natriuresis works in reverse at low pressure.

why.correct: Juxtaglomerular cells release renin, cells between the tubules release EPO, and tubule cells make calcitriol by activating vitamin D. ADH, aldosterone and ANP are made elsewhere and act on the kidney.
options: Correct. Renin comes from the juxtaglomerular cells.
ADH is made by the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.
Correct. The kidney releases EPO when its oxygen supply falls.
Aldosterone comes from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex.
Correct. Kidney tubule cells complete the activation of vitamin D.
ANP comes from stretched atrial muscle cells.

why.correct: Aldosterone adds sodium channels, potassium channels and pumps to principal cells. They reabsorb more sodium and secrete more potassium.
options: ANP does the reverse for sodium: more sodium and water in the urine.
PTH controls calcium and phosphate, not sodium and potassium.
ADH controls water, through aquaporins; it does not directly swap sodium for potassium.
Correct. Aldosterone keeps sodium and loses potassium.

why.correct: PTH removes sodium–phosphate symporters from the proximal tubule, so phosphate is lost, and increases calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule, so less calcium is lost per unit filtered. (Over time, blood calcium rises so much that more calcium is filtered, and urine calcium can rise despite PTH.)
options: Correct. PTH keeps calcium and loses phosphate.
This reverses both of PTH's kidney effects.
That pattern belongs to ANP-like or anti-aldosterone effects, not PTH.
PTH does not act on the collecting duct's water permeability; that is ADH's role.

why.correct: Nitrite comes from bacteria converting nitrate, and leukocyte esterase comes from white blood cells. With burning and urgency but no fever or flank pain, the infection is most likely in the bladder (cystitis), not yet the kidney.
options: A stone typically causes severe wave-like flank pain and blood in the urine, not positive nitrite and leukocyte esterase.
Correct. Bacteria plus white cells, with bladder symptoms.
AKI is recognized by rising creatinine and falling urine output, not by burning and urgency.
Stress incontinence is leakage with coughing or lifting. It does not cause burning or positive nitrite.

why.correct: Sweat loss raised her plasma osmolarity and lowered her volume, so ADH rose. Water left her collecting ducts into the medulla, and the urine became small in volume and concentrated, with the urochrome packed into less water.
options: A blocked duct would stop urine flow; she is making urine, just concentrated.
Correct. A specific gravity of 1.030 is the concentrated end of the normal range.
Protein would show on the dipstick; specific gravity alone points to concentration.
Too little ADH makes large volumes of dilute urine with a low specific gravity.

why.correct: Oliguria (olig- = little) is less than about 400 mL a day in an adult. 250 mL is below that but above the 50 to 100 mL cutoff for anuria.
options: Polyuria is more than about 3 L a day.
Correct. 250 mL is between the anuria cutoff and 400 mL.
Anuria is almost no urine, less than 50 to 100 mL a day.
Normal output is about 1 to 2 L a day.

why.correct: A rise in arterial pressure raises pressure around the tubules, the proximal tubule pulls its sodium–hydrogen exchangers from the membrane and reabsorbs less, sodium and water are excreted, and the lower volume brings pressure back down: negative feedback without any hormone.
Cells between the kidney tubules make EPO. As CKD destroys kidney tissue, EPO falls, and the bone marrow makes fewer red cells. EPO injections treat it.
options: Red cells are too large to pass a healthy or diseased filter in large numbers; that is not the cause of her anemia.
Correct. Low EPO leads to low red cell production.
Retained wastes can shorten red cell life a little, but the main cause is low EPO, not destroyed marrow.
Renin affects blood pressure through the RAAS; it doesn't control red cell production.

why.correct: Without dialysis, his kidneys can't excrete potassium. Hyperkalemia depolarizes cardiac cells and disturbs conduction, which can cause a fatal arrhythmia within hours. It needs emergency treatment and dialysis.
options: Anemia develops over weeks and is not what makes two missed sessions an emergency.
Bone disease develops over months to years.
Correct. Potassium at 7.2 threatens the heart now.
Itching is unpleasant but not life-threatening in the short term.

why.correct: Dialysate contains no urea, so urea diffuses down its gradient from the blood into the dialysate, not the other way.
options: This step is right. The membrane separates blood from dialysate.
This step is right. Dialysate flows past the other side.
This is the error. Urea moves from blood, where it is high, into dialysate, where it is absent.
This step is right. Dialysate has little potassium, so potassium leaves the blood.
This step is right. Pressure pulls extra water out of the blood.

why.correct: Stones form when solutes become concentrated enough to crystallize. A larger urine volume keeps calcium and oxalate diluted below that point.
options: Correct. Dilute urine is the main prevention.
Cutting dietary calcium lets more oxalate be absorbed from the gut and can raise the risk; normal calcium intake is advised.
Loop diuretics raise calcium in the urine. A thiazide, which lowers it, is the diuretic used.
More concentrated urine raises the risk of crystals forming.

why.correct: Leakage with a jump in abdominal pressure, without urgency, is stress incontinence: the pelvic floor and external urethral sphincter, often weakened by childbirth, can't hold. Pelvic floor training strengthens them.
options: Urge incontinence comes with a sudden strong urge from an overactive detrusor. She has none.
Overflow incontinence is constant dribbling from a bladder that can't empty.
Correct. Pressure-triggered leakage with a weak pelvic floor.
Functional incontinence happens when the urinary tract works but the person can't reach a toilet.

why.correct: Vomiting lowered his blood volume, and his kidneys were relying on prostaglandins to widen the afferent arterioles and protect GFR. Ibuprofen blocks prostaglandin synthesis, the afferent arterioles narrow, and GFR falls: acute kidney injury.
options: Correct. Removing the prostaglandin protection lowered GFR.
Blocking NKCC2 is what loop diuretics do, not ibuprofen.
Ibuprofen does not work by raising ADH, and ADH alone lowers urine volume without raising creatinine.
Ibuprofen doesn't form stones in the ureters.

why.correct: U × V is the amount excreted per minute. Dividing it by the plasma concentration gives the volume of plasma that contained that amount: the clearance.
options: Correct. P, in the same units as U.
GFR is not in the formula. For inulin, the clearance you calculate equals GFR.
Specific gravity measures how concentrated urine is, not how much plasma is cleared.
V is already a rate per minute, so time is built in.

why.correct: The problem was too little blood reaching healthy kidneys. That is prerenal AKI, which reverses when perfusion is restored.
options: Postrenal AKI comes from blocked urine outflow, such as a stone or blocked bladder outlet.
Chronic kidney disease lasts more than 3 months; hers came on suddenly and recovered.
Intrinsic AKI means the kidney tissue itself is damaged; hers was healthy.
Correct. Low perfusion of healthy kidneys.

why.correct: Urea is a single carbon double-bonded to an oxygen, with two nitrogen groups. The liver makes it from ammonia, and it is the largest solute in urine.
options: Correct. One carbon, one oxygen, two nitrogen groups.
Ammonia is the smallest molecule on the figure: one nitrogen with three hydrogens.
Uric acid is the large molecule with two fused rings.
Creatinine is not shown on this figure.
